# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. Both tools offer features such as messaging, file sharing, and video conferencing, making them ideal for remote teams, businesses, and communities. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch from Slack to Element is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack has a monthly fee per user.
* Data ownership: Element allows users to have full ownership and control over their data, while Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Slack is generally easier to set up.
* Scalability: Slack is designed to handle large teams and organizations, while Element may require more configuration to scale.
* Feature difference: Element has end-to-end encryption for all conversations, while Slack only offers encryption for certain types of data.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Large user base and community
* Integrates with many third-party apps
* Offers a free plan with limited features
* Has a user-friendly interface
* Limited control over data and security
* Can be expensive for large teams
* Limited customization options
* Dependent on Slack's servers and infrastructure
### Element
* Free and self-hosted
* Offers end-to-end encryption for all conversations
* Allows for full control over data and security
* Customizable and extensible
* Can be more cost-effective for large teams
* Requires technical expertise to set up and maintain
* Limited support for certain features and integrations
* May require more configuration to scale
* Limited user base and community compared to Slack

## When to Choose Each
### Slack
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and don't mind paying a monthly fee per user. It's ideal for small to medium-sized teams, startups, and businesses that need a simple and intuitive communication platform. Slack is also a good choice for teams that don't require advanced security features or customization options.
### Element
Element is a good choice for teams that require full control over their data and security, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining their own servers. It's ideal for large teams, enterprises, and organizations that need advanced security features and customization options. Element is also a good choice for teams that are looking for a cost-effective solution and are comfortable with self-hosting.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack export tool, which provides a JSON file containing your team's messages, files, and other data.
2. Set up your Element server and configure it to your needs.
3. Use the Element import tool to import your Slack data into Element.
4. Configure your Element instance to match your team's needs, including setting up user accounts, channels, and integrations.
5. Test your Element instance to ensure that everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is a promising alternative to Slack, but it may not be production-ready for most users right now. While it offers many advanced features and customization options, it requires technical expertise to set up and maintain, which can be a barrier for many teams.
One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching to Element is that it may not have the same level of support for certain features and integrations as Slack. For example, Element may not have the same level of support for third-party apps and services as Slack.
Overall, we recommend Element for teams that require advanced security features and customization options, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining their own servers. However, for teams that prioritize ease of use and don't mind paying a monthly fee per user, Slack may still be the better choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need advanced security features and are looking for a cost-effective solution.
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that require more control over their data and security, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining their own servers.
* Large teams (more than 50 users) that need advanced security features and customization options, and are looking for a cost-effective solution.
* Teams that don't need integration with third-party apps and services.
* Teams that are comfortable with self-hosting and have the technical expertise to set up and maintain their own servers.

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and self-hosted, which means you can use it without paying a monthly fee per user. However, you will need to pay for your own server costs and maintenance.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain than Slack. However, once set up, Element can be just as easy to use as Slack.
### Can I integrate Element with third-party apps and services?
Yes, Element has a range of integrations with third-party apps and services, including GitHub, Trello, and Google Drive. However, the range of integrations may not be as extensive as Slack's.
### Is Element secure?
Yes, Element offers end-to-end encryption for all conversations, which means that only the sender and recipient can read the messages. Element also allows for full control over data and security, which can be a major advantage for teams that require advanced security features.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can migrate your Slack data to Element using the Slack export tool and the Element import tool. However, the migration process may require some technical expertise and configuration.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are communication platforms designed for team collaboration, offering a range of features including chat, file sharing, and integrations. This comparison is beneficial for teams and organizations considering a switch from Slack to Mattermost, particularly those prioritizing data ownership and cost-effectiveness. The core use case for both tools is team communication, and a key reason to switch would be to gain more control over data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Slack charges per user, while Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option.
* Data ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, whereas Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup complexity: Slack is generally easier to set up, with a more user-friendly interface, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Both platforms are scalable, but Mattermost's self-hosted option gives teams more flexibility to scale according to their needs.
* Integration with GitHub: Slack has a more seamless integration with GitHub, while Mattermost's integration requires more setup and configuration.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Slack:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Good mobile app support
* Large user community
* Limited control over data storage and security
**Mattermost:**
* Self-hosted option for full data control
* Customizable and extensible through plugins and APIs
* Free, open-source option
* Steeper learning curve due to self-hosting requirements
* Limited support for certain integrations, such as GitHub

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations, and are willing to pay for these features. It is particularly suitable for small to medium-sized teams with simple communication needs. On the other hand, Mattermost is a better option for teams that require full control over their data and are comfortable with self-hosting and customization. This includes large enterprises with complex security requirements and open-source projects that value community involvement.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack export tool, which provides a JSON file containing your team's messages, files, and other data.
2. Set up a Mattermost server, either self-hosted or through a cloud provider.
3. Use the Mattermost import tool to import your Slack data, which supports JSON files exported from Slack.
4. Configure your Mattermost instance to match your team's needs, including setting up plugins and integrations.
5. Test your Mattermost instance to ensure a smooth transition for your team.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready alternative to Slack for many users, offering a self-hosted option and customizable plugins. However, it is essential to consider the technical limitations, such as the need for self-hosting expertise and potential integration gaps. For teams that value data control and cost-effectiveness, and are willing to invest time in setup and customization, Mattermost is a viable option.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not need advanced integrations
* Open-source projects that value community involvement and customization
* Large enterprises with complex security requirements and data control needs
* Teams with limited budgets that cannot afford Slack's per-user costs
* Developers who prefer self-hosting and customization options

## FAQ
### Can I use Mattermost for free?
Yes, Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, which allows teams to host their own servers and have full control over their data.
### Is Mattermost compatible with Slack integrations?
Mattermost has a range of integrations with third-party apps, but some Slack integrations may not be compatible or require additional setup.
### How do I export my Slack data?
You can export your Slack data using the Slack export tool, which provides a JSON file containing your team's messages, files, and other data.
### Can I use Mattermost on mobile devices?
Yes, Mattermost has mobile apps for both Android and iOS, allowing teams to stay connected on-the-go.
### Is Mattermost suitable for large teams?
Yes, Mattermost is scalable and suitable for large teams, with self-hosting options providing flexibility and control over data storage and security.

# Discord vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Discord and Element are communication platforms designed for community building and team collaboration. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and organizations looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source alternative, with the core use case being secure and customizable communication. The key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce dependence on third-party services.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Discord offers a free plan with limitations, while Element is free and self-hosted, with costs limited to server maintenance.
* Data ownership: Element allows users to retain full ownership of their data, whereas Discord's data ownership is subject to its terms of service.
* Setup complexity: Discord is generally easier to set up, with a more streamlined onboarding process, while Element requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Element is highly scalable, with the ability to support large communities and teams, while Discord's scalability is limited by its proprietary infrastructure.
* Feature difference: Element supports end-to-end encryption for all communications, while Discord only offers encryption for direct messages.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $9.99/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $4.99/month (billed annually) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $4.99/month (billed annually) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Discord
* Pros:
  + Easy to set up and use
  + Large user base and community support
  + Rich media support and integrations
  + Mobile apps for on-the-go access
* Cons:
  + Limited customization options
  + Data ownership concerns
  + Limited scalability
  + Proprietary infrastructure
### Element
* Pros:
  + Self-hosted and open-source
  + End-to-end encryption for all communications
  + Highly customizable and scalable
  + Retain full ownership of data
* Cons:
  + Steeper learning curve for self-hosting
  + Limited mobile app support
  + Requires technical expertise for setup and maintenance
  + Limited support for rich media and integrations

## When to Choose Each
Discord is suitable for small to medium-sized teams and communities that prioritize ease of use and don't require advanced customization or data ownership. It's ideal for gaming communities, social groups, and small businesses with simple communication needs. On the other hand, Element is designed for larger organizations, enterprises, and communities that require high levels of customization, scalability, and data ownership. It's perfect for teams that need advanced security features, such as end-to-end encryption, and are willing to invest time and resources into setup and maintenance.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Discord data using the Discord API or a third-party tool, such as discord-exporter, which supports JSON and CSV formats.
2. Set up an Element server, either self-hosted or through a hosting provider, and configure the necessary settings and integrations.
3. Import your exported data into Element using the Element API or a compatible import tool, such as element-importer.
4. Configure your Element instance to match your Discord setup, including channels, roles, and permissions.
5. Test your Element instance to ensure a smooth transition and resolve any issues that may arise during the migration process.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires significant technical expertise for setup and maintenance. However, for organizations and communities that value data ownership and advanced security features, Element is a viable alternative to Discord. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's mobile app support is limited, and users may experience issues with push notifications and offline access.

Element's self-hosted nature and open-source license make it an attractive option for teams that require high levels of customization and control. However, the setup process can be complex, and users may need to invest significant time and resources into configuring their instance. Despite these limitations, Element is a promising platform that offers a unique combination of security, scalability, and customization.

For teams that prioritize ease of use and don't require advanced customization, Discord remains a suitable option. However, for organizations that value data ownership and advanced security features, Element is a clear choice. We recommend that teams with 50+ users and complex communication needs consider switching to Element, while smaller teams and social groups may find Discord more suitable.

## Who Should Switch
* Large enterprises with 100+ users that require advanced security features and data ownership
* Communities with 500+ members that need high levels of customization and scalability
* Teams with complex communication needs, such as multiple channels and roles, that require a self-hosted solution
* Organizations that prioritize data ownership and are willing to invest time and resources into setup and maintenance
* Developers and technical teams that require a highly customizable and open-source communication platform

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and open-source, with costs limited to server maintenance and upkeep.
### Is Element compatible with Discord?
No, Element is not directly compatible with Discord, but you can export your Discord data and import it into Element using compatible tools.
### Does Element support end-to-end encryption?
Yes, Element supports end-to-end encryption for all communications, including messages, voice, and video calls.
### Can I self-host Element?
Yes, Element is designed for self-hosting, and you can set up your own instance on your preferred server or hosting provider.
### Is Element suitable for small teams?
Not necessarily, Element is designed for larger organizations and communities that require advanced customization and scalability, but smaller teams may find it too complex and resource-intensive.

title: Notion vs AppFlowy

# Notion vs AppFlowy

## Overview

Notion is a popular all-in-one workspace combining notes, wikis, databases, and project management. AppFlowy is an open-source alternative with a local-first architecture that keeps your data on your device or own server.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; AppFlowy is completely free
- **Data location**: AppFlowy stores data locally by default; Notion stores on their servers
- **Offline support**: AppFlowy works fully offline; Notion requires internet for most features
- **Privacy**: AppFlowy does not collect usage data; Notion privacy policy allows data analysis
- **Feature parity**: Notion has more polished features and AI tools; AppFlowy is rapidly catching up

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | AppFlowy |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | GPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### AppFlowy

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [AppFlowy-IO/AppFlowy](https://github.com/AppFlowy-IO/AppFlowy) * ~59k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion suits teams wanting a polished workspace with AI writing tools and seamless collaboration without managing infrastructure.

**Choose AppFlowy if:** AppFlowy is ideal for privacy-conscious individuals, users in regions with data sovereignty requirements, or anyone needing offline-first functionality.

## Migration Path

Export your Notion workspace as Markdown plus CSV files, then import the Markdown files into AppFlowy. Database structures will need to be recreated manually.

## Our Take

AppFlowy is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Notion tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your AppFlowy instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Notion, switching to self-hosted AppFlowy will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Notion until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is AppFlowy free to use?
Yes. AppFlowy is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to AppFlowy?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the AppFlowy import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does AppFlowy get regular updates?
Yes. AppFlowy has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use AppFlowy without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if AppFlowy development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Notion](https://notion.so) and [AppFlowy](https://appflowy.io) before making decisions.*

## Overview

# GitHub vs GitLab (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and GitLab are two popular version control platforms that help developers manage their codebase. This comparison is beneficial for development teams, especially those considering switching from GitHub to GitLab due to concerns about data ownership or scalability. The core use case for both tools is source code management, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data or to reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers free accounts with limited features, while GitLab offers a free self-hosted option with more features.
* Data ownership: GitLab allows users to self-host their repositories, giving them full control over their data, while GitHub stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: GitLab can be more complex to set up, especially for self-hosted options, while GitHub is generally easier to get started with.
* Scalability: GitLab is designed to handle large-scale deployments and offers more features for enterprise users, while GitHub can become expensive for large teams.
* Feature difference: GitLab offers built-in CI/CD pipelines, while GitHub requires third-party integrations for similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|----------|---------|

## When to Choose Each

## Our Take
GitLab is a production-ready alternative to GitHub for most users, offering a wide range of features and scalability. However, one technical limitation to consider is that GitLab's self-hosted option can be complex to set up and manage, requiring significant technical expertise. For teams that prioritize data ownership and security, GitLab is a clear choice, but for small teams or those already invested in the GitHub ecosystem, GitHub may still be the better option.

# GitHub vs Gitea

## Overview

The world largest code hosting and collaboration platform. Owned by Microsoft since 2018. is a popular proprietary tool in the developer-tools space. Gitea is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub costs Free / $7-$21/user; Gitea is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: GitHub is Proprietary; Gitea is MIT
- **Data ownership**: Gitea can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Gitea eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Gitea has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | Gitea |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Gitea

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [go-gitea/gitea](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea) * ~44k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Gitea if:** Gitea is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from GitHub in its standard export format, review Gitea import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Gitea is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Gitea instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted Gitea will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Gitea free to use?
Yes. Gitea is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to Gitea?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the Gitea import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Gitea get regular updates?
Yes. Gitea has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Gitea without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Gitea development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [Gitea](https://gitea.io) before making decisions.*
